## Example 2.4 {#ss2-example-2-4}

Prove algebraically that if the $n$th partial sum of a sequence is the $n$th perfect square, then the sequence is the sequence of odd numbers.

<p class="booklet-cue">Booklet p. 8 · Example 2.4 · Complete the proof in your booklet.</p>

::: notes
Preserve the source task. Given S_n=n², first check a_1=S_1=1. For n≥2:

a_n=S_n−S_{n−1}=n²−(n−1)²=n²−(n²−2n+1)=2n−1.

Thus the sequence is 1,3,5,7,…, the positive odd numbers. The formula also agrees with the separately checked first term. Distinguish a proof for every valid n from checking a few numerical differences. The growing-square diagram explains the same difference geometrically. Do not introduce the general arithmetic-series formula yet.
:::
